_comment: A tiny hand-written knowledge base of astronomy facts. This is the 'KG' in RAG+KG. Add your own facts here — each one is a small, verifiable statement the model should prefer over its own recall. No database required; it's just JSON.

facts.text: A heliocentric orbit is described by six Keplerian elements: semi-major axis a (size), eccentricity e (shape), inclination i (tilt to the ecliptic), longitude of ascending node Omega, argument of perihelion omega, and mean anomaly M (position along the orbit at an epoch).

Osculating elements are the instantaneous orbit at one epoch and oscillate under planetary perturbations. Proper elements are nearly-invariant averaged quantities (proper a, e, sin i) valid over millions of years. Asteroid families are identified by CLUSTERING IN PROPER ELEMENT SPACE, not osculating elements.

An asteroid family is a group of minor bodies sharing similar proper orbital elements because they are collisional fragments of a common parent body. Families are found with Hierarchical Clustering Method (HCM) in proper (a, e, sin i) space.

The Themis family is a large collisional family in the outer main belt near semi-major axis a ~= 3.13 AU. Its members are primarily C-type (carbonaceous), and water-ice frost and a comet-like activity have been detected on some members (e.g. 24 Themis, 133P/Elst-Pizarro).

The Koronis family sits in the outer main belt (a ~= 2.87 AU). Members are S-type (silicaceous). 243 Ida (visited by Galileo, has the moon Dactyl) is a Koronis member. Members show a curious clustering of spin-axis orientations (the 'Slivan states').
The Eos family is an inclined family in the outer main belt (a ~= 3.01 AU, sin i ~= 0.18). Members are predominantly the rarer K-type spectral class, intermediate between S- and C-types.

The Vesta family ('vestoids') are inner-belt fragments (a ~= 2.36 AU) blasted off the crust of 4 Vesta by the Rheasilvia impact. They are V-type (basaltic) and are the parent source of the HED (howardite-eucrite-diogenite) meteorites.
The Flora family is a large, diffuse inner-belt family (a ~= 2.2 AU) of S-type asteroids. It is a leading candidate source region for the L-chondrite meteorites.

Kirkwood gaps are depleted zones in the main-belt semi-major-axis distribution at mean-motion resonances with Jupiter (e.g. the 3:1 at a ~= 2.50 AU, 5:2 at 2.82 AU, 2:1 at 3.27 AU). Resonant pumping of eccentricity clears asteroids from these zones.

The Yarkovsky effect is a small nongravitational thermal force that slowly changes an asteroid's semi-major axis (prograde rotators drift outward, retrograde inward). It spreads asteroid families in 'a' over time, so the V-shape of a family in (a, size) space is used to estimate the family's age.

Near-Earth Objects are grouped by orbit into Atiras (interior to Earth), Atens (a < 1 AU, cross Earth), Apollos (a > 1 AU, cross Earth) and Amors (approach but don't cross). A Potentially Hazardous Asteroid (PHA) has a minimum orbit intersection distance <= 0.05 AU and absolute magnitude H <= 22.

The Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) is the 10-year survey conducted at the Vera C. Rubin Observatory on Cerro Pachon, Chile. It uses an 8.4 m (6.5 m effective) telescope with a 3.2-gigapixel camera and a 9.6 square degree field of view.

Over its 10-year survey LSST is expected to catalog roughly 5 million main-belt asteroids, ~100,000 NEOs, ~10,000+ trans-Neptunian objects, and thousands of comets — increasing the number of known solar system small bodies by an order of magnitude.

LSST issues a real-time alert for every source that changes brightness or position, ~10 million alerts per night, within 60 seconds of exposure. Alerts are distributed through community brokers (e.g. ANTARES, ALeRCE, Fink, Lasair) that filter and classify them.

Difference Image Analysis (DIA) subtracts a deep static template from each new exposure so only things that changed remain. It is how LSST detects moving objects and transients: a real moving asteroid leaves a positive residual that shifts between visits.

Single-night detections of a moving object are linked into a 'tracklet'; tracklets across several nights are linked into a 'track' and fit to a preliminary orbit (the Moving Object Processing System heritage, HelioLinC3D for Rubin). digest2 scores how likely a tracklet is a NEO.

An asteroid's absolute magnitude H is its brightness at 1 AU from both Sun and observer at zero phase angle. Diameter follows from H and the geometric albedo p_V: D(km) = 1329 / sqrt(p_V) * 10^(-H/5). Albedo separates dark C-types (p_V ~ 0.05) from bright S/V-types (p_V ~ 0.2-0.4).

Main-belt taxonomy from reflectance colors: C-types (dark, carbonaceous, dominate the outer belt), S-types (silicaceous, dominate the inner belt), X-types (metallic/enstatite, ambiguous albedo), plus smaller V, K, L, D classes. LSST's six ugrizy filters give coarse colors for taxonomic sorting at survey scale.
